title: The Mortara affair (1858)
hookLine: a Jewish boy is taken from his parents in Bologna

cards: Evening, in a house in Bologna. Momolo and Marianna Mortara have put their children to bed. There is a knock.
Police of the Papal States are at the door, with an order to take one of the boys, Edgardo. The parents beg. They are given a little time, and then the boy is carried out of the house.
His family will spend years trying to bring him back. Today's story is hard, and it is told here plainly.

teach.h: THE POPE AS A WORLDLY KING.
teach.b: Bologna was then ruled by the pope as a worldly king, and church law was the law of the land. Under that law, a child who had been baptized a Catholic could not be raised by Jewish parents.
The family had a Christian servant girl.
She said that years before, when Edgardo was a baby and very sick, she had secretly sprinkled water on him and said the words of baptism, afraid he would die. She told no one at the time.

When the story reached church officials, they ruled the boy was now a Catholic, and sent the police. Edgardo was taken to Rome and raised in a house for converts, under the protection of Pope Pius the Ninth himself.
Jewish communities in other countries took up the case. Newspapers across Europe and in America printed it, and readers who were not Jewish were troubled too. Governments sent protests.
The pope refused to send him home. The ending is harder still. Edgardo grew up inside the Church and became a Catholic priest.

When the Papal States later fell, he was old enough to choose, and he chose to stay. He never returned to his parents' faith. Jews remember the case as a wound, and Catholic writers have argued about it in their own way.
The Torah knows a father's grief like this. When Jacob is told his son Joseph is gone, he tears his clothes and mourns, while the boy is alive and far away in a foreign land.

teach.h: AND HIS FATHER WEPT FOR HIM.
teach.b: Genesis gives that grief one short line: "And his father wept for him."

how: Jewish historians and teachers retell the Mortara case as part of the story of emancipation, and it is often studied alongside the fight for religious freedom and the rights of parents.

games.q: you are Edgardo's father. the papal police have taken your son to Rome. what do you do?
o: travel, write and plead for him.
leave Bologna and never speak of it.
games.why: Momolo Mortara traveled and pleaded, Jewish communities abroad took up the case, and still the pope refused to send the boy home.

practice: Bring Edgardo's family to mind: his father traveling and writing, his mother at home, the other children in the next room.
Think of anyone you know who is waiting for someone who hasn't come home, and hold the waiting for a moment without trying to end it. If you pray, you can remember them in your own words.
